claim: E. coli cells were grown in M9 minimal media supplemented with glycerol, glucose, or glucose and eight amino acids, resulting in doubling times of 89, 53 and 41 min, respectively.
source: We used M9 minimal media supplemented with glycerol, glucose or glucose and eight amino acids, resulting in doubling times of 89, 53 and 41 min, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript directly reports measured doubling times for different growth media conditions.

claim: The heritability of birth length between mother and daughter is characterized by a Pearson correlation coefficient of r≈0.5.
source: also in agreement with the adder model, the heritability of birth length between mother and daughter is characterized by a Pearson correlation coefficient of r≈0.5 (see Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific correlation coefficient value from their data analysis.

claim: Adder behavior is observed at slow growth conditions.
source: Our own observations are thus in line with this later study and it should also be noted that Si et al. (2019) only found a weak deviation from adder behavior when reanalyzing the data of Wallden et al. (2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations and comparison with published literature.

claim: The initiation length Li and birth length Lb are clearly correlated in all conditions.
source: However, as can be seen in Figure 2A, we observe that the initiation length Li and birth length Lb are clearly correlated in all conditions, rejecting the initiation mass model.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 2A showing correlation between these variables.

claim: The initiation mass model is rejected by the observed correlation between initiation length and birth length.
source: However, as can be seen in Figure 2A, we observe that the initiation length Li and birth length Lb are clearly correlated in all conditions, rejecting the initiation mass model.
evidence: The authors use their experimental data to reject a specific model based on observed correlations.

claim: The absence of an initiation mass has been shown by Adiciptaningrum et al. (2016) and confirmed in a recent comprehensive analysis (Micali et al., 2018a).
source: The absence of an initiation mass has already been shown by Adiciptaningrum et al. (2016) and confirmed in a recent comprehensive analysis (Micali et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim references prior published work that supports the finding.

claim: The double-adder model accurately reproduces measured distributions and correlations at all growth rates.
source: As can be seen in Figure 5, the double-adder model accurately reproduces measured distributions and correlations at all growth rates.
evidence: The manuscript presents simulation results in Figure 5 that match experimental data.

claim: The global adder behavior for cell size regulation naturally emerges from the double-adder model.
source: In particular, the global adder behavior for cell size regulation naturally emerges from it (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript shows through simulations that the model produces the observed adder behavior.

claim: The double-adder model reproduces the distribution of the number of origins at birth.
source: Furthermore, the distribution of the number of origins at birth, which reflects the presence of overlapping replication cycles is also reproduced (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript shows simulation results matching experimental data for origin number distribution.

claim: The three fundamental variables (growth rate, dΛif, and dΛid) fluctuate independently around their averages for each individual cell cycle.
source: In particular, we assume that these three variables fluctuate independently around these averages for each individual cell cycle, and that all other parameters such as the sizes at birth, initiation, and the times between birth and division or between initiation and division, are all a function of these three fundamental variables.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this assumption as part of the model definition.

claim: The double-adder decomposition has the highest independence (I=0.882) among replication-centric models for experimental data.
source: Of all replication-centric models, our double-adder model clearly reaches the highest independence
evidence: The manuscript presents statistical analysis results in Figure 7 showing the double-adder model has the highest independence score.

claim: Division-centric models accomplish lower independence than replication-centric models.
source: We find in general that none of the division-centric models accomplishes high independence.
evidence: The manuscript presents comparative statistical analysis in Figure 7 showing lower independence scores for division-centric models.

claim: The decomposition analysis successfully identifies the model used in simulations as having the highest Independence I.
source: As shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4, the decomposition analysis successfully identifies the model used in the simulation as having the highest Independence I.
evidence: The manuscript validates their analysis method by applying it to simulated data with known model.

claim: The double-adder model is the most successful at explaining experimental measurements in the dataset from Si et al. (2019).
source: As shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5, here again the double-adder model is the most successful at explaining the experimental measurements.
evidence: The manuscript applies their analysis to an independent published dataset and shows consistent results.

claim: Origins always occupy the position of future division sites (mid-cell, 1/4 and 3/4 positions etc.) when replication is initiated.
source: One remarkable observation that is well known within the field (Lau et al., 2004; Nielsen et al., 2006) and that we also observe in our data (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1), is that origins always occupy the position of future division sites (mid-cell, 1/4 and 3/4 positions etc.) when replication is initiated.
evidence: The manuscript reports their own observation of this phenomenon and cites prior literature.

claim: A double-adder mechanism similar to the one proposed for E. coli has been shown to explain cell cycle control in mycobacteria.
source: Interestingly, a double-adder mechanism similar to the one that we propose here has been shown to explain cell cycle control in mycobacteria (Logsdon et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work showing similar mechanisms in other bacteria.

claim: Mycobacterial cell cycles exhibit adder behavior for both division and replication starting at initiation.
source: Despite those important differences, it was shown that mycobacterial cell cycles exhibit adder behavior for both division and replication starting at initiation, in a manner highly similar to our observations in E. coli.
evidence: The manuscript references published findings about mycobacterial cell cycle control.

claim: The mechanism connecting replication and division must be quite fundamental and independent of the specifics of available genes and their expression.
source: This suggests that the mechanism connecting replication and division must be quite fundamental and independent of the specifics of available genes and their expression.
evidence: The authors infer this conclusion from the observation of similar mechanisms in different bacterial species.

claim: An adder for the regulation of replication initiation can be implemented at the molecular level by having a 'sensor' protein that builds up at each origin and triggers replication initiation when a critical mass is reached.
source: As others have pointed out previously (Ho and Amir, 2015), an adder for the regulation of replication initiation can be easily implemented at the molecular level by having a 'sensor' protein that builds up at each origin, and that triggers replication initiation whenever a critical mass is reached at a given origin.
evidence: The manuscript discusses a potential molecular mechanism based on prior theoretical work.

claim: If a sensor protein is homeostatically controlled such that its production relative to overall protein production is kept constant, then the average volume per origin will be kept constant across conditions.
source: If this sensor protein is additionally homeostatically controlled such that its production relative to the overall protein production is kept constant, then the average volume per origin will also be kept constant across conditions.
evidence: The manuscript presents a theoretical argument about how homeostatic control could maintain constant volume per origin.

claim: Acidic phospholipids accumulate in the cell membrane at future division sites where they interact with components of the division machinery.
source: At the molecular level, the common triggering of initiation and polymerization might be explained by the accumulation of acidic phosholipids in the cell membrane precisely at future division sites (Renner and Weibel, 2011) where they probably interact with components of the division machinery.
evidence: The manuscript cites published work about phospholipid localization and proposes a speculative mechanism.

claim: Acidic phospholipids play a role in promoting replication by rejuvenating the initiator protein DnaA-ADP into DnaA-ATP.
source: At the same time those lipids are known to play a role in promoting replication by rejuvenating the initiator protein DnaA-ADP into DnaA-ATP (Saxena et al., 2013), and might therefore be a 'hub' coordinating the two cycles.
evidence: The manuscript cites published work about the role of phospholipids in DnaA activation.

claim: Acidic phospholipids might be a 'hub' coordinating the replication and division cycles.
source: At the same time those lipids are known to play a role in promoting replication by rejuvenating the initiator protein DnaA-ADP into DnaA-ATP (Saxena et al., 2013), and might therefore be a 'hub' coordinating the two cycles.
evidence: The authors speculate about a potential coordinating role based on known functions of phospholipids.

claim: The strain used is derived from the K-12 strain BW27378, a Δ(araH-araF)570(::FRT) derivative of the Keio collection background strain.
source: All strains are derived from the K-12 strain BW27378, a Δ(araH-araF)570(::FRT) derivative of the Keio collection background strain (Baba et al., 2006) obtained from the Yale Coli Genetic Stock Center.
evidence: The manuscript describes the bacterial strain used in the experiments.

claim: A 250 lacO repeats FROS array with chloramphenicol resistance was inserted close to the origin of replication in the asnA gene.
source: A 250 lacO repeats FROS array with chloramphenicol resistance was inserted close to the origin of replication in the asnA gene by λ-Red recombination and P1 transduction resulting in strain GW273.
evidence: The manuscript describes the genetic modification made to create the experimental strain.

claim: Cells were grown in a Mother Machine type microfluidic device and imaged by time-lapse microscopy.
source: To achieve this, cells were grown in a Mother Machine type microfluidic device (Wang et al., 2010) and imaged by time-lapse microscopy.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental setup used for data collection.

claim: The replication cycle was monitored by detecting initiation as the duplication of an oriC proximal FROS tagged locus imaged by fluorescence microscopy.
source: The replication cycle was monitored by detecting initiation as the duplication of an oriC proximal FROS tagged locus imaged by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method used to monitor replication initiation.

claim: Origin splitting can be affected by a cohesion time.
source: This of course only offers a proxy for initiation timing, as origin splitting can be affected by a cohesion time (Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation of their measurement method based on published work.

claim: Cell radius is assumed to be constant and cell length is used as a proxy for cell volume.
source: As done previously, we assume that cell radius is constant and use cell length as a proxy for cell volume (Adiciptaningrum et al., 2016; Taheri-Araghi et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript states an assumption used in their analysis, citing prior work that used the same assumption.

claim: The average number of replication origins per unit of cellular volume is approximately constant across conditions.
source: For example, in the specific case of E. coli that we study here, it has long been known that growth rate, cell size, and replication initiation are coordinated such that the average number of replication origins per unit of cellular volume is approximately constant across conditions (Donachie, 1968)
evidence: The manuscript cites a well-established observation from the literature.

claim: Cellular volume grows approximately exponentially with growth rate.
source: or that cellular volume grows approximately exponentially with growth rate (Taheri-Araghi et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published observation about the relationship between cell volume and growth rate.

claim: E. coli cells maintain a constant average size by following an adder strategy.
source: Several recent studies have focused on understanding the regulation of cell size, resulting in the discovery that E. coli cells maintain a constant average size by following an adder strategy
evidence: The manuscript references the established finding of adder behavior in E. coli.

claim: The adder model efficiently dampens large cell size fluctuations caused by intrinsically noisy regulation without the need for any fail-safe mechanism.
source: A remarkable feature of the adder model is its capacity to efficiently dampen large cell size fluctuations caused by the intrinsically noisy regulation, without the need for any fail-safe mechanism.
evidence: The manuscript describes a theoretical property of the adder model.

claim: The adder strategy is shared by various bacterial species, archaea, and some eukaryotes such as budding yeast.
source: This efficient strategy has been shown to be shared by various bacterial species as well as by archea (Eun et al., 2018) and even some eukaryotes such as budding yeast (Soifer et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work showing adder behavior across different organisms.

claim: Most models assume that the accumulation of a molecular trigger, usually assumed to be DnaA, leads to replication initiation, which in turn controls the corresponding future division event.
source: Broadly, most models assume that the accumulation of a molecular trigger, usually assumed to be DnaA, leads to replication initiation, which in turn controls the corresponding future division event (Campos et al., 2014; Ho and Amir, 2015; Wallden et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes common assumptions in existing models from the literature.

claim: The time between replication initiation and division is roughly constant across a range of conditions.
source: The observations that cell volume grows exponentially with growth rate (Schaechter et al., 1958) and that, across a range of conditions, the time between replication initiation and division is roughly constant (Helmstetter et al., 1968) led Donachie to propose that the volume per origin of replication is held constant (Donachie, 1968).
evidence: The manuscript cites a classic observation from the literature.

claim: The growth rate is correlated (r≈0.3) between mother and daughter.
source: As has been observed previously (Campos et al., 2014) the growth rate is correlated (r≈0.3) between mother and daughter.
evidence: The manuscript reports an observed correlation and cites prior work showing the same.

claim: Accounting for mother-daughter correlation in growth rate was found not to be critical for capturing features of E. coli cell cycle.
source: Accounting for this mother-daughter correlation in growth rate was found not to be critical for capturing features of E. coli cell cycle, but was included in the model to reproduce simulation conditions of previous studies.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from their simulation analysis.

claim: Purely geometric division models such as the Harris and Theriot (2016) model have been challenged by research indicating that surface expansion is coupled to dry-mass increase rather than to volume increase.
source: It should also be noted that purely geometric division models such as the Harris and Theriot (2016) model have been recently challenged more broadly by research indicating that surface expansion is coupled to dry-mass increase rather than to volume increase (Oldewurtel et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent published work that challenges certain types of models.

claim: Micali et al. (2018b) introduced a class of models in which replication and division cycles are controlled by two concurrently running processes coupled through a check-point.
source: Recently, Micali et al. (2018b) introduced a wider class of models in which the replication and division cycles are controlled by two concurrently running processes, which are coupled through a check-point that demands a certain minimal amount of time has to elapse between replication initiation and division.
evidence: The manuscript describes a class of models from published literature.

claim: If the cell cycle is controlled by independent control processes, then the variables associated with these control processes should fluctuate independently.
source: The basic idea behind this approach is that, if the cell cycle is controlled by independent control processes, then we expect the variables associated with these control processes to fluctuate independently.
evidence: The manuscript presents the theoretical basis for their statistical analysis approach.

claim: The independence of fluctuations in added volume from fluctuations in other variables constitutes the support of the adder mechanism.
source: It is precisely this independence of fluctuations in added volume from fluctuations in the other variables, that constitutes the support of the adder mechanism.
evidence: The manuscript explains the theoretical basis for identifying adder behavior.

claim: The independence per definition ranges from 0 to 1 (perfect independence).
source: Thus, the independence per definition ranges from 0 to 1 (perfect independence).
evidence: The manuscript defines the range of their independence measure.

claim: The residual dependence in the double-adder model might result from correlated errors in measurements or reflect some small biological dependence not captured by the model.
source: This residual dependence might either result from correlated errors in the measurements, or it might reflect some small biological dependence not captured by our model.
evidence: The authors speculate about possible explanations for observed discrepancies between model and data.

claim: The double-adder model does not require an exponential relationship between average cell-size and average growth rate.
source: It should be noted that, whereas models based on a timer between initiation and division naturally predict the well-known exponential increase of average cell-size with average growth rate measured in the bulk (Schaechter et al., 1958; Taheri-Araghi et al., 2017), the double-adder does not require such a relationship.
evidence: The manuscript discusses a theoretical property of their model in comparison to timer models.

claim: The difference between a timer and adder model is in the nature of the correlations of different cell cycle quantities across single cells within one condition, not in the behavior of their averages across conditions.
source: The difference between a timer and adder model is in the nature of the correlations of different cell cycle quantities across single cells within one condition, and not in the behavior of their averages across conditions.
evidence: The manuscript explains a key conceptual distinction between model types.

claim: The two adders connected to replication initiation are sufficient to recapitulate both cycles without explicitly enforcing constraints reflecting mechanisms such as over-initiation control by SeqA and nucleoid occlusion.
source: While the division and replication cycles are seemingly coupled, our analysis demonstrates that two simple adders connected to replication initiation are sufficient to recapitulate both cycles without explicitly enforcing constraints reflecting mechanisms such as over-initiation control by SeqA and nucleoid occlusion which ensures that division only occurs after chromosome replication is completed.
evidence: The manuscript presents a conclusion from their modeling and simulation work.

claim: The initiation-to-initiation adder mimics SeqA activity by creating a refractory period without initiation.
source: The initiation-to-initiation adder mimics SeqA activity by creating a refractory period without initiation, and the initiation-to-division adder ensures that a minimal time is allocated for replication to complete.
evidence: The manuscript explains how their model implicitly captures known biological constraints.

claim: The initiation-to-division adder ensures that a minimal time is allocated for replication to complete.
source: The initiation-to-initiation adder mimics SeqA activity by creating a refractory period without initiation, and the initiation-to-division adder ensures that a minimal time is allocated for replication to complete.
evidence: The manuscript explains how their model implicitly captures known biological constraints.

claim: Si et al. (2019) proposed that division and replication cycles are only seemingly connected and used perturbation methods to drive cells to states where the uncoupling is revealed.
source: In the course of our study, new research proposed that division and replication cycles are only seemingly connected, and used perturbation methods to drive cells to states where the uncoupling is revealed (Si et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript describes findings from a concurrent published study.

claim: Cells driven to a filamentous state recover normal sizes through successive single division events seemingly independently from initiation and following an adder behaviour.
source: Another recent study (Wehrens et al., 2018) using a perturbative approach has shown that cells driven to a filamentous state recover normal sizes through successive single division events seemingly independently from initiation and following an adder behaviour.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings from a published study.

claim: Division inhibition hinders replication related processes such as chromosome segregation.
source: As division inhibition also hinders replication related processes such as chromosome segregation (Sánchez-Gorostiaga et al., 2016), it is difficult to untangle the different mechanisms that might be at play.
evidence: The manuscript cites published work about the effects of division inhibition.

claim: Division is driven by the polymerization of the FtsZ ring and its progressive constriction.
source: It is well known that division is driven by the polymerization of the FtsZ ring, which includes a host of other FtsZ-ring associated proteins, and its progressive constriction.
evidence: The manuscript states established knowledge about bacterial cell division.

claim: FtsZ and other division proteins are heavily regulated at several levels.
source: Although this is conceivable, that is it is known that FtsZ and other division proteins are heavily regulated at several levels (Dewar and Dorazi, 2000)
evidence: The manuscript cites published knowledge about FtsZ regulation.

claim: In slow growth conditions, FtsZ concentration varies during the cell cycle.
source: and that especially in slow growth conditions its concentration varies during the cell cycle (Männik et al., 2018)
evidence: The manuscript cites published observations about FtsZ concentration dynamics.

claim: Recent data suggest that FtsZ concentration is constant during the cell cycle.
source: Moreover recent data (Si et al., 2019) rather suggest that FtsZ concentration is constant during the cell cycle.
evidence: The manuscript cites recent published findings about FtsZ concentration.

claim: At replication initiation, some local molecular event occurs that will eventually trigger division at the same site.
source: This observation not only suggests that, at replication initiation, some local molecular event occurs that will eventually trigger division at the same site, but it is also remarkably consistent with the idea of an adder running only between replication initiation and division.
evidence: The authors infer a molecular mechanism from observed spatial-temporal patterns.

claim: Some molecular event that occurs during replication initiation triggers the start of FtsZ ring formation, and the timing from initiation to division is controlled by the polymerization dynamics of the FtsZ ring.
source: One long-standing idea that is consistent with these observations is that some molecular event that occurs during replication initiation triggers the start of FtsZ ring formation, and that the timing from initiation to division is controlled by the polymerization dynamics of the FtsZ ring (Weart and Levin, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript describes a speculative molecular mechanism from the literature.
